newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-WellPoint sees signing Midwest business.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-WellPoint sees signing Midwest business.

text.p: WellPoint Health Networks Inc in the next few days expects to announce the signing of some large Midwest employer accounts, the company's chief executive said on Thursday.
"We're hoping that this thing will be resolved this week ... It should be in the next couple of days," Leonard Schaeffer said during an interview in Chicago with Reuters.
Flush from a recent run-up in its share price and freed from a regulatory quagmire that had held it back for years, the $4.2-billion-in-revenue managed-care concern is expanding.
From its California base, WellPoint has moved into Texas and is targeting growth in Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Georgia, New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.

Schaeffer said WellPoint is not a typical holding company for health maintenance organizations. Rather than growing by buying other HMOs, WellPoint so far has made its two biggest acquisitions in traditional, fee-for-service health insurance.

In April 1996, it bought the life and health unit of Massachusetts Mutual for $380 million. Last March, it bought John Hancock Mutual's health and life unit for $86.7 million -- both with the goal of moving their members to managed care.
"That's the value-creation principle," Schaeffer said. "When Aetna Inc bought U.S. HealthCare, they paid $3,800 a member. When we bought John Hancock, we paid $87 per member," he said.
"HMO members are very profitable, but they cost a lot of money. The fee-for-service members that we bought aren't profitable, but we can fix it. We can create value," he said.

When buying a fee-for-service book of business, Schaeffer said WellPoint expects to lose up to 30 percent of its member base as the transition to managed care occurs. Unprofitable members are priced out and some others jump ship. "If we don't lose that, it's all gravy," he said.

WellPoint is one of the most profitable managed care concerns in the country. Its medical loss ratio -- a measure of the portion of premium revenues paid out to cover members' medical costs -- was 78.8 percent in the first quarter.

Following industry trends, that figure was up from the year-ago period, when it was 74.9 percent. But Schaeffer said WellPoint's ratio in California, where it has mature provider networks, declined in the first quarter from a year earlier.
"Where we have proprietary networks, we're controlling costs. Where we don't, we're seeing a higher rate of (cost) increase," Schaeffer said.

Inside California, WellPoint is seeing its medical costs rise one or two percent this year. "Outside California, we expected five percent or so, but I think it's higher. I think it's maybe seven to 10 percent," he said.

"The problem is John Hancock and Mass Mutual are 99 percent not in our networks. So we're seeing a higher trend than we expected. It won't have a big effect on our bottom line because our expectations for their contribution this year were very minimal," he added.

WellPoint, based in Woodland Hills, a Los Angeles suburb, was formed in 1992 as a for-profit unit of Blue Cross of California. A complex regulatory dispute followed and was finally resolved last year. Since then, WellPoint shares have climbed to 48-1/8 from a range in the high 20s a year ago.
